title: Keep intoxication arrestees out of city jail, family says
article: Although he was homeless, Doug Morissette spoke to his daughter almost daily.
Madison Murtland remembers her late father as a hard-working man with a big sense of humour who would playfully tease her during their nightly phone conversations.
"He just had an energy about it that made you feel good," she said in an interview Tuesday.
After Morissette's arrest for public intoxication on Jan. 15, 2013, the 57-year-old died alone in a police detention cell.
An inquiry into his death this week heard that Morissette died of an overdose of alcohol and methadone.
His family says while the father of two was known to carry around a mickey of vodka in his front pocket, he was never one to mess with any hard drugs.
Now they want answers about why his overdose wasn't recognized by police or medical staff at the detention centre.
"When people read stories like this, they think, 'it's just another drunk.' They don't understand that it's a person," said Kelly Murtland, Morissette's exwife.

Murtland said Morissette had been on the streets for the better part of a decade. His backpack with his clean clothes and a toothbrush slung over his back, he would sleep in homeless shelters or on friends' couches.
Frequently he would be arrested for public intoxication and would find shelter in the Saskatoon police detention cells.
Murtland said she never thought those cells would be his final resting place.
"It's almost like he had been surviving for that many years and you just think he is going to keep surviving," Murtland said.

She and her daughter sat through two days of testimony this week at the inquest into Morissette's death. They heard how no one - from the arresting officers to the paramedics in detention - saw that Morissette was at risk of an overdose the night he died.

"I am positive I asked him two times. He denied any drug use or taking any substances," testified Joel Kinzel, the MD Ambulance paramedic who was on duty in the police detention unit on the night of Morissette's death.
Kinzel was part of a pilot project that assigns paramedics to the police detention unit in order to help prevent deaths in custody.
Kinzel testified that he did not do a "physical assessment" of Morissette when he was booked into the cells.

Murtland and her daughter said they believe things would have been much different if Morissette had never been arrested in the first place. At the time of his death, Madison was pregnant and Morissette was only months away from becoming a grandfather.

"What would have happened if an ambulance answered that call? ... it would have been a totally different scenario," Kelly Murtland said. "They shouldn't use the city jails as a drunk tank. They aren't the type of people who are going to look after someone like that."
